newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Romania's new president free from communist past.
newsitem.headline: Romania's new president free from communist past.

text.p: Emil Constantinescu, a former Bucharest University rector who won Romania's presidency on Monday, is a principled politician untainted by a communist past.
Constantinescu, a centrist reformer, ousted ex-communist Ion Iliescu in a stunning shift in Romania's political scene, ending a long period of dominance by leftists.
Iliescu's defeat completed a hat-trick of victories by Constantinescu's Democratic Convention bloc (CDR) in local, parliamentary and presidential elections.
It ensured the first real transfer of political power since the 1989 revolt which ousted late dictator Nicolae Ceausescu.
"It is a victory for millions of Romanians who have hoped for this change since December 1989," Constantinescu said, elated at a triumph he did not expect even a month ago.

A former geology professor, the bearded academic was drafted into the political front line by the CDR because of his untarnished reputation. Although a Communist party member under Ceausescu he played no active role.
"There are no dark corners in my life and consequently I cannot be blackmailed," Constantinescu said during the campaign. "Nobody can put pressure on me."
Constantinescu, 57 on Tuesday, became CDR leader in 1992, the year when he was soundly beaten by Iliescu in his first attempt to win the presidency.

Since 1992, the committed anti-communist who was one of the few teachers to join students in December 1989 street protests that overthrew Ceausescu has gathered enough experience to outplay Iliescu at the political game.

Bringing down Iliescu, a shrewd career politician who portrayed himself as the only person capable of ensuring stability in a country that often suffered post-communist turmoil, was no easy task for Constantinescu.
But after an initial setback in August when leftist smears that he was a closet monarchist appeared briefly to stick Constantinescu showed he had learned to campaign.

A new professionalism emerged which made a political virtue of the strong moral streak that motivated his entry into public life. He attacked corruption fiercely and said he would stay close to Romania's people as president.
He promised his supporters he would lead Romania to a confident future, but acknowledged dragging the country from poverty could be painful.

"I ask you to be at my side for the true awakening of Romania. I call on you to discover together this new age...we will not destroy, we will continue to build," Constantinescu told thousands of cheering supporters in a victory speech.
He ignored Iliescu's claim his inexperience would hamper him and vowed to work with whoever necessary to revive a weak economy that has left most Romanians in dire poverty.
He pledged to begin a reform programme immediately he is inaugurated.
His party campaign was based on pledge to step down in 200 days if it failed to cut taxes, improve living standards and modernise decaying industries.
